title: West Nile virus epidemic years predicted next-year decreases of crows, other corvids and chickadees in US bird surveys in 2000-2024; the link became weaker after 2008 and summer heat did not show it
abstract: Question: after the 1999 invasion, do West Nile virus (WNV) epidemic years still decrease susceptible bird species in the next year, and does summer heat decrease them only after the virus arrived? Data: CDC human neuroinvasive WNV cases per million by US state and year (exposure W = log10(1 + cases per million)), USGS Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes 1966-2025 and Project FeederWatch winter feeder counts 1988-2024 as two independent observation systems, and GHCN-CAMS summer temperature. Method: next-year change of a focal group minus control species on the same route or feeder site, same observer, with year and state fixed effects, state-clustered intervals and a state block bootstrap; a plan was written before the outcome models. Results: per unit of W, the next-year BBS change was -0.086 [-0.129, -0.043] for American Crow, -0.072 for other corvids and -0.113 for chickadees and titmouse; robin and bluebird showed no link. FeederWatch repeated the signs: crow -0.302 [-0.368, -0.236], corvids -0.121, parids -0.175. Control species did not decrease. The BBS link was largest in 2000-2008 and clearly weaker after 2008 for crows and corvids. The FeederWatch crow link stayed negative in each period. The BBS dose response was monotonic, with clear decreases above 3 cases per million. Heat increased W, but the route heat slope did not become more negative after WNV arrived; the implied heat effect (about -0.005 per 1 C) is below the power of the data. Limitations: human cases are a coarse state-level proxy for bird transmission; the design is correlational; the BBS lead term was negative for corvids, a partial failure of the timing test; the FeederWatch robin and bluebird decrease failed the timing test and is not interpreted as a WNV effect.

Right: slope of next-year change (focal minus control species, log units) per unit of state WNV index W, for four bird groups, all years and three periods. Blue: Breeding Bird Survey (June counts); orange: FeederWatch (winter counts). Bars are 95% state-clustered intervals.

Left: joint model with WNV index of the season before the pair (prior), between the two counts (between) and after the second count (next). Only 'between' should predict change. Right: BBS slope of next-year change on June-August temperature anomaly before WNV (1967-1998) and after WNV arrival (2002-2024).
BBS next-year change (focal minus control) by class of state neuroinvasive WNV cases per million, relative to state-years with zero cases, 2000-2024, with 95% state-clustered intervals.

citations.reason: First large-scale BBS evidence of WNV-related decreases of crows and other species after arrival. We show that later epidemic years also predict decreases and that the effect became weaker after 2008.
Found persistent WNV impacts on many species. Our FeederWatch crow result agrees with a continuing effect; our BBS results show a weaker effect after 2008.
GHCN-CAMS land air temperature for June-August anomalies.
North American Breeding Bird Survey 1966-2025 release (States.zip, Weather.csv, Routes.csv, SpeciesList.csv).
Project FeederWatch raw data, May 2024 release.
CDC ArboNET WNV human cases by state and year, 1999-2025.
US Census state population estimates for cases per million.
Only prior campaign publication on WNV; it forecasts human disease counts from the same CDC table. We use the human counts as an exposure for birds.
Shows weather-related detection artefacts in BBS counts; motivated our same-observer, control-species difference design and the independent FeederWatch check.
